claims.claim: Martin says there is no college of heralds enforcing heraldry in the Seven Kingdoms.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, So Spake Martin "Heraldry in Westeros", westeros.org (1999-04-13)
claims.quote: no college of heralds for enforcement

claims.claim: Martin says individual knights and lords in Westeros have a certain amount of freedom to bear what shields they prefer.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, So Spake Martin "Heraldry in Westeros", westeros.org (1999-04-13)
claims.quote: freedom to bear what shields they prefer

claims.claim: Martin illustrates Westerosi differencing by Mace Tyrell's second son Ser Garlan bearing two roses on his shield when brothers fight on the same field.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, So Spake Martin "Heraldry in Westeros", westeros.org (1999-04-13)
claims.quote: Ser Garlan (the second son) with two roses on his shield

claims.claim: Martin says Big and Little Walder quarter the arms of their mother's and grandmother's houses on their shields and surcoats though they could lawfully wear the Frey towers unadorned.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, So Spake Martin "Heraldry in Westeros", westeros.org (1999-04-13)
claims.quote: quarter the arms of their mother's and grandmother's houses

claims.claim: Martin grounds the looseness of Westerosi heraldry in the Dark Ages and early Middle Ages, when he says heraldry was unregulated and a matter of individual choice.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, So Spake Martin "Heraldry in Westeros", westeros.org (1999-04-13)
claims.quote: heraldry was unregulated and very much a matter of individual choice

claims.claim: Martin says some of the old Kings in the North undoubtedly had their own personal heraldic variants but that he has not yet decided what they were.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, So Spake Martin "Heraldry in Westeros", westeros.org (1999-04-13)
claims.quote: though I haven't yet decided what they were

claims.claim: Martin says Jack Vance is a great writer, period, and deserves a place in the canon of American literature.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, "The Genius of Jack Vance", Not a Blog (2009-07-17)

claims.claim: Martin says Vance had a huge influence on him and his work.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, quoted in "George R.R. Martin on Jack Vance", Harper Voyager UK blog (2013-06-03), relaying Not a Blog
claims.quote: had a huge influence on me and my work

claims.claim: Martin calls Maurice Druon France's best historical novelist since Dumas Pere.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, "Maurice Druon's THE IRON KING", georgerrmartin.com (2013-03-30)
claims.quote: France’s best historical novelist since Dumas Pere

claims.claim: Reviewer Stefan Raets says Martin uses chapter-to-chapter perspective switching with great success to show complex intrigues from various points of view.
claims.source: Stefan Raets, Reactor/Tor.com review of THE IRON KING (2013-03-12)
claims.quote: a technique writers like Martin use with great success
claims.page: review body, paragraph on narrative voice

claims.claim: Raets says Druon's occasional ominous-sounding omniscient narrator immediately makes the novel sound more dated.
claims.source: Stefan Raets, Reactor/Tor.com review of THE IRON KING (2013-03-12)
claims.quote: occasionally uses an ominous-sounding omniscient narrator
claims.page: review body, paragraph on narrative voice

claims.claim: Raets says Druon refers to some characters sometimes by name, sometimes by title and sometimes by the territory they control, sending the reader back to the character list.
claims.source: Stefan Raets, Reactor/Tor.com review of THE IRON KING (2013-03-12)
claims.quote: sometimes by the territory they control

claims.claim: Raets says Druon's characters occasionally explain past events to people who do not need them explained, which makes the book sound dated.
claims.source: Stefan Raets, Reactor/Tor.com review of THE IRON KING (2013-03-12)
claims.quote: explain past events to people who don’t need them explained
claims.page: review body, paragraph on narrative voice

claims.claim: Martin writes in his foreword to the 2013 HarperCollins edition of The Iron King that the Starks and the Lannisters have nothing on the Capets and the Plantagenets.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin's Foreword to THE IRON KING, quoted by Stefan Raets, Reactor/Tor.com (2013-03-12)
claims.quote: the Starks and the Lannisters have nothing on the Capets

claims.claim: Medievalist Michael Livingston says Martin does not engage in one-to-one associations between the real world and his fictional one.
claims.source: Michael Livingston, "Getting Medieval on George R. R. Martin", Reactor/Tor.com (2015-07-16)
claims.quote: Martin doesn’t engage in one-to-one associations
claims.page: body, paragraph on the Wars of the Roses
